newsitem.title: UK: Gold Outlook - market braces for testing week.
newsitem.headline: Gold Outlook - market braces for testing week.

text.p: Precious metals prices slumped to their lowest levels in around three years last week leaving market professionals unconvinced they had seen the bottom of the current downward spiral.
"This market is heading for $360. That's the view on this desk anyway," said one London-based dealer of the gold price's medium term future.
Markets were influenced all week by the U.S. four-day Thanksgiving holiday which led to cautious dealing up to Wednesday and relatively thin markets on Thursday and Friday.
On Thursday gold fell to $372.20, its lowest fix since April 25 1994 when it was $370.25, and slipped lower again on Friday.

A recovery on Friday could have prompted fresh interest for New York's return this week but instead speculators and professionals made a concerted effort to push the market lower. But it held around $371.50.
"We are so close to a round number ($370.00) that this is inevitably going to be suggested as a target," a dealer said.
Bearish pressure has been building on gold for weeks as heavy selling variously said to be on behalf of central banks and Austrialian and South African producers hit the market.
"Producers seem to have decided this is not just a blip but that the price will continue to fall," said bullion analyst Andy Smith of Union Bank of Switzerland.

Market confidence was eroded also by fears of European central bank selling in the run up to European Monetary Union and confirmation the IMF would sell gold reserves if it failed to raise funds to help poorest nations by other means.

A fresh tremble came when a director of the ultra gold-conservative Swiss National Bank voiced the opinion that Switzerland should reduce the level of gold backing for its currency from 40 percent, opening the possibility of selling or lending formerly inactive gold reserves.
Analysts estimate world central banks and other institutions hold over 35,000 tonnes of gold in their reserves, the vast bulk of which is kept well away from the market.
More anxiety came with news that Russia's Finance Ministry will take over sales of domestic gold output, interpreted to mean that Russia would become a more willing exporter.
"These structural movements in thinking have made the market nervous and rightly so," one analyst said.
A harrowing week could be coming for gold with U.S. stock markets showing no sign of falling and the dollar still strong against other major currencies.
"A hefty fall in the Dow, or the dollar coming off will be needed to get some interest in gold again," one dealer said.

Other precious metals suffered too. Silver fell in gold's wake to its lowest since March 28 1995 at $4.7275 while platinum and palladium slipped to lows reaching back over three years. Platinum's fix of $374.25 on November 28 was its lowest since December 3 1993 and sister metal palladium hit $114.25, its lowest since April 20, 1993.
"Demand usually picks up at this time of year but it hasn't. Inventories are high, the funds are short and going shorter and available material cannot be absorbed," one dealer explained.
